name: Albert Camus
role: French-Algerian novelist, essayist and journalist (1913-1960), Nobel laureate
summary: Camus, writer of The Stranger and The Rebel, was an anti-totalitarian libertarian socialist: he campaigned against the death penalty, defended freedom against Soviet-style revolution, sided with the workers' movements and refused to justify murder for distant ends.

sources.title: Reflections on the Guillotine (1957), English translation, The Anarchist Library
sources.author: Albert Camus
sources.usedFor: His case for immediate abolition of the death penalty.

sources.title: Bread and Freedom (1953 talk at the Bourse du Travail, Saint-Etienne, first printed in La Revolution proletarienne), The Anarchist Library
sources.author: Albert Camus
sources.usedFor: Freedom and justice, the workers' movements, Soviet socialism.

sources.title: Neither Victims nor Executioners, 'Toward Dialogue' (Combat, 30 November 1946), The Anarchist Library
sources.author: Albert Camus
sources.usedFor: Refusing to compromise with murder as a means to far-off ends.

sources.title: The Rebel (1951; trans. Anthony Bower, Penguin Modern Classics), Internet Archive full text
sources.author: Albert Camus
sources.usedFor: State terror and revolution, revolutionary trade unionism, the Commune, limits to rebellion, murder as necessary and inexcusable.

sources.title: Algerian Chronicles (Actuelles III, 1958; trans. Arthur Goldhammer, Harvard University Press, 2013), Internet Archive full text
sources.author: Albert Camus
sources.usedFor: His federal plan for Algeria, the civilian truce, torture, the Arab peoples.

sources.title: Speech at the Salle Wagram meeting on Hungary, 15 March 1957 ('Kadar a eu son jour de peur'), French text with notes, Le Grand Continent
sources.author: Albert Camus

notes: First audit. The Algerian writings were not reachable as full text, so the answers rest on The Rebel and three essays: Reflections on the Guillotine, Bread and Freedom and the last Combat article of Neither Victims nor Executioners. The Anarchist Library's The Human Crisis (1946 New York lecture) and The Guest (a short story) were read and settle none of the statements. The Rebel was read from the Internet Archive text (a Penguin edition with a foreword by Herbert Read, whose words are not cited) by theme: state terror, revolution, the Commune, trade unionism, murder and limits. Algerian Chronicles was read from the Internet Archive text by theme (Camus's own pieces, not the translator's introduction), and the 1957 Hungary speech from the Grand Continent reprint. Wikipedia-only claims about Algeria, the Spanish Civil War and his break with Sartre are not used.
